summary.text: Plankton are living things that drift in water or air and cannot push themselves against currents or wind.
Because the group is defined by how it lives and moves rather than by ancestry, it spans every major kingdom, from bacteria to jellyfish.
Plankton form the base of the marine food web, and the plant-like phytoplankton among them produce roughly half of Earth's oxygen.

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: From microscopic bacteria up to jellyfish

items.prompt: A jellyfish can pulse and swim slowly. Why is it still counted among the plankton?

options.label: It is closely related to drifting algae
It cannot generally overpower the currents
It spends its adult life on the sea floor
It makes its own food from sunlight

items.explain: Plankton are defined by being unable to beat the currents. Jellyfish swim, but not fast enough to generally overcome them.

items.prompt: Roughly how much of Earth's oxygen production comes from microscopic phytoplankton?

options.label: About 5 percent
About 20 percent
About half
Nearly all of it

items.explain: Phytoplankton photosynthesis accounts for roughly half of Earth's oxygen production.

items.prompt: The eastern Atlantic next to the dry Sahara is rich in phytoplankton. What best explains this?

options.label: Desert dust blown out to sea supplies iron
Rivers from the desert add fresh water
Desert heat warms the sea to ideal levels
Few fish live there to graze on them

items.explain: Iron reaches the ocean mainly as dust settling on the surface, and trade winds carry Saharan dust over the eastern Atlantic, feeding phytoplankton.

items.prompt: Large areas of the tropical open ocean get strong sunshine all year, yet produce relatively little plankton growth. Why?

options.label: The water there is too warm for photosynthesis
Strong waves keep plankton from settling
Too many whales eat the plankton there
Nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate are scarce

items.explain: Light is not enough on its own: these regions offer limited nutrients like nitrate, phosphate and silicate, so primary production stays relatively low.

items.prompt: A young sea urchin drifts in open water as a larva, then settles on the sea floor for the rest of its life. How does it fit the plankton?

options.label: It is plankton for its entire life
It is plankton for only part of its life
It never counts, since it ends on the floor
It counts only once it reaches the floor

items.explain: Meroplankton, such as sea urchin larvae, drift only for part of their lives before moving to a swimming or sea-floor existence.

items.prompt: Far below the depth where sunlight allows photosynthesis, zooplankton and bacteria still live. What do they mainly feed on?

options.label: Algae growing in the faint deep light
Sand and rock grains on the sea floor
Organic material sinking from the waters above
Nothing; they survive without eating

items.explain: At depths with no primary production, zooplankton and bacterioplankton consume organic material that sinks from more productive surface waters, known as marine snow.

beats.title: Drifters That Feed the Sea
beats.hook: A bacterium and a jellyfish share the same label, and it has nothing to do with their family tree.

beats.prompt: Match each group of sea life to how it lives

right.label: Drifts, unable to swim against currents
Floats on or near the surface
Lives on the deep sea floor

beats.explain: These names sort sea life by where it lives and how well it moves, not by what kind of organism it is.

beats.prompt: Sort each drifter by how it gets its food
beats.explain: Phytoplankton such as diatoms and cyanobacteria make their own food, while zooplankton such as radiolarians and copepods eat other organisms.

beats.prompt: Trade winds carry dust from the Sahara out over the eastern Atlantic. What happens to the phytoplankton in those waters?
beats.explain: Iron mainly reaches the ocean as dust settling on the surface, so waters beside unproductive, arid land like the Sahara typically have abundant phytoplankton.

choices.label: They are sparse, smothered by the dust
choices.feedback: Dust sounds harmful, but it delivers iron, a nutrient phytoplankton need.

choices.label: They are abundant, fed by iron in the dust
They are sparse, since dry land nearby adds nothing
choices.feedback: It seems an arid coast should mean barren water, but the wind-borne dust is the supply.

choices.label: They are unaffected, since only light matters
choices.feedback: Light is the main driver, but nutrients such as iron also limit growth.

steps.text: The main cause of differences in plankton abundance is the availability of light.
Large areas of the tropical oceans receive abundant light.
Light is all phytoplankton need, so nothing else can hold them back there.
So those tropical waters should be among the most productive anywhere.

beats.explain: Nutrients are a second limit: tropical and subtropical waters with plenty of light still have relatively low production because nitrate, phosphate and silicate are limited.

beats.idea: Plankton are defined by drifting with the currents rather than by ancestry, and together they form the base of the marine food web.

paragraphs.heading: Drifters of the water
paragraphs.text: Plankton are living things that drift in water, or in air, and cannot push themselves against a current or the wind. The name comes from a Greek word for a drifter or wanderer. A single one is called a plankter. Some, like jellyfish, can swim slowly, but generally not fast enough to beat the currents.

paragraphs.heading: Defined by lifestyle, not family
paragraphs.text: The group is set by where an organism lives and how well it moves, not by its family tree. So plankton come from all the major kingdoms of life, from microscopic bacteria, archaea and algae up to jellyfish and ctenophores. Swimmers strong enough to fight a current are called nekton instead, and creatures living on the deep sea floor are called benthos. Organisms floating on or near the surface are called neuston.

paragraphs.heading: Four ways to eat
paragraphs.text: Plankton were traditionally split into two feeding groups. Phytoplankton, such as diatoms and cyanobacteria, make their own food, while zooplankton, such as copepods and radiolarians, eat other living things the way animals do. Research has shown that many single cells, including many dinoflagellates, both photosynthesize and swallow food, so a third group, the mixoplankton, is now recognised. A fourth group, the decomposers, includes bacterioplankton, microscopic fungi and viruses, which recycle nutrients so other plankton can use them as food again.

paragraphs.heading: Small but essential
paragraphs.text: Plankton smaller than about a millimetre keep aquatic ecosystems healthy and balanced. Phytoplankton produce roughly half of Earth's oxygen and play a major role in locking away carbon. Marine microorganisms may make up 70 to 90 percent of the living mass in the ocean, and they largely drive the biological pump, which pulls carbon dioxide from the air and sends carbon down to deeper water. Taken together, plankton are the foundation of the marine food web, feeding species from forage fish to baleen whales.

paragraphs.heading: Light first, then nutrients
paragraphs.text: How many plankton live in a place changes from region to region, with depth and with the seasons. Light is the main reason. Nearly all plankton ecosystems are powered by sunlight, which keeps almost all of their production in surface waters and in places and seasons with plenty of light. Nutrients come second. Much of the tropical and subtropical ocean has lots of light but little nitrate, phosphate and silicate, so production there is relatively low.

paragraphs.heading: Iron from desert dust
paragraphs.text: Some ocean regions hold plenty of the main nutrients and are still unproductive. They are short of the micronutrient iron, and adding it can set off blooms of phytoplankton. Iron mostly reaches the ocean as dust settling on the sea surface. So, oddly, waters next to dry, barren land are often rich in phytoplankton, as in the eastern Atlantic, where trade winds carry dust from the Sahara.

paragraphs.heading: Lifelong drifters and visitors
paragraphs.text: Holoplankton spend their whole lives as plankton; most algae, copepods and salps are examples. Meroplankton drift for only part of their lives, usually as larvae, and later either swim freely or live on the sea floor. Most fish, along with sea urchins, starfish, crustaceans and marine worms, start out this way as larvae.
